records.name: Cameroon
records.summary:
Cameroon is dangerous for trans visitors. The Shakiro case is the defining documentation: in February 2021, trans women Shakiro and Patricia were arrested in a Douala restaurant for the clothes they were wearing, convicted of “attempted homosexuality,” “indecent dressing” and ID irregularities, and sentenced to five years. They described five months of “hell” in Douala's central prison, initially in leg chains, before release pending appeal; Shakiro later received asylum in Belgium. Article 347-1 criminalises same-sex acts (up to 5 years), and Cameroon has among Africa's highest prosecution rates.

Police and mob violence against perceived LGBT people are both documented, and there is no legal gender recognition or protection of any kind. The Shakiro conviction shows that visible trans expression in a public place is itself treated as a prosecutable offence.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation in public risks arrest on indecency/ID grounds; prison conditions are severe.

sources.claim: BBC (May 2021): two trans women in Cameroon, including trans celebrity YouTuber Shakiro, were sentenced to five years in prison for 'attempted homosexuality', outraging public decency and ID-card problems - the maximum term. Lawyer Alice Nkom: 'The message is clear: homosexuals don't have a place in Cameroon.' Cameroon is among 31 African countries criminalising gay sex.

Wikipedia biography of Shakiro (b. 1997), Cameroonian trans activist: arrested and charged with 'attempted homosexuality' in 2021, sentenced to five years; fled Cameroon later that year, hid in Nigeria, and received asylum in Belgium in 2023.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Cameroon: documents discrimination against gays and lesbians among societal abuses, alongside security-force killings, torture, harsh prisons, and arbitrary arrests - the criminalisation context (Article 347).
Human Rights Watch (May 2022): 'Cameroon: Rising Violence Against LGBTI People' — documents mob violence and killings amid inflammatory rhetoric.
CNN (Jan 2013): report on two gay men freed in Cameroon after being jailed for appearing effeminate.

freshness.fact: Both male and female same-sex activity remains criminalised and prosecuted aggressively (unchanged since the 2021 BBC and 2009 US reports).

records.name: DR Congo
records.summary:
DR Congo is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised — but the reality on the ground is severe insecurity: mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented, police extortion is routine, the east is an active conflict zone (M23), and LGBT organisations (Savie asbl in Bukavu) report systematic violations in their 2024 UPR submission. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure; Kinshasa's small scene is underground.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but outing risks mob violence with no effective state protection anywhere in the country.

sources.claim: Stakeholder submission to the DRC's 5th-cycle UPR (March 2024) by Savie asbl NGO and others: the DRC does not criminalise same-sex relations but neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights; public displays of same-sex affection can be prosecuted under indecent-exposure provisions (Article 176 of the Penal Code: 'anyone who publicly outrages morals by actions...').

Human Rights Watch (Dec 2017): 'DR Congo: Rebels Were Recruited to Crush Protests' — child soldiers reportedly recruited by a militia to suppress opposition demonstrations; general human-rights context for the security environment, not LGBT-specific.

GayOut travel guide for DR Congo: rates the country 'High Risk for LGBTQ+' - no explicit national criminalisation but Article 176 ('indecent acts') and local ordinances applied to LGBTQ people; armed militia groups in eastern DRC have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity; state authority collapse means legal protections are theoretical.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror) on LGBTQ rights in the DRC: same-sex activity legal for both sexes (never outlawed, even under Belgian rule), equal age of consent; but no gender-identity recognition, no relationship recognition (same-sex marriage banned constitutionally since 2006), limited protections; church groups promote the view that homosexuality is immoral; public same-sex affection can trigger prosecution under indecency provisions.

Queer In The World travel guide: 'LGBT Rights In Congo: Everything You Should Know Before You Visit' - travel-oriented overview of the legal situation and safety considerations for LGBTQ visitors to the DRC.

freshness.fact: Same-sex activity legal; public-indecency provisions still occasionally used for prosecution; no anti-discrimination law — UPR-era (2025) sources remain accurate.

evidence.title: LGBTQ rights in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

records.name: Republic of the Congo
records.summary: Republic of the Congo is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised); EUAA COI (2024) documents societal discrimination, police harassment, and absence of protection; no LGR; small underground community.

sources.claim: EUAA COI Query Response Q29-2024 (May 2024) on the Republic of the Congo: situation of LGBTIQ people covering legislation and implementation, treatment by the state and society, availability of state protection, and access to support services, for the period January 2022 to May 2024. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised but public-expression provisions are applied; state protection is limited.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for the Republic of the Congo: official assessment including the SOGI section - same-sex conduct not criminalised, but societal discrimination documented; no legal gender recognition.
US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for the Republic of the Congo: official assessment including the SOGI section - continuing societal discrimination and absence of protections.

freshness.fact: Homosexuality legal (2005 code removed criminalisation) but no protections, with documented discrimination/abuse — consistent with the EUAA 2024 query response cited.

records.name: Cook Islands
records.summary:
A self-governing island state in free association with New Zealand, the Cook Islands criminalised male same-sex acts under a 1969 colonial-era Crimes Act (terms to seven or ten years, consent no defence) until parliament repealed the provisions in April 2023, effective 1 June 2023 — after a decade of stalled bills, NZ-assisted drafting, and sustained advocacy by the local Te Tiare Association, whose spokespeople called the laws 'draconian' colonial relics. Enforcement in living memory was essentially absent; the repeal removed a held-over risk rather than an active prosecution threat.

Pre-contact history reframes the present: 2020 coverage noted a nation 'historically accepting of same-sex relationships' whose anti-LGBT sentiment arrived with colonisation. Post-decriminalisation there is still no marriage equality and no general non-discrimination statute; public life is strongly church-inflected; the islands are some 15,000 people where everyone is known — decriminalised, unequal, and small.

sources.claim: PinkNews (April 2023): the Cook Islands decriminalised homosexuality - parliament voted to remove the 'indecent acts between males' provision (up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act, never enforced); the Crimes Amendment Bill took effect 1 June 2023, described as 'a historic day'.

PinkNews (Oct 2020): decriminalisation plans stalled again - the parliament deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months; sex between men was punishable by up to 7 years; the nation was historically accepting of same-sex relationships but anti-LGBT sentiment arrived with colonisation.

PinkNews (Aug 2017): the Cook Islands moved to decriminalise - the draft Crimes Bill (drafted with New Zealand help) would remove sections 154-155 (up to 7 years for gay sex, 5 for 'indecent act', consent explicitly no defence); Te Tiare Association member Valentino Wichman called the provisions 'draconian' colonial relics.

RNZ Pacific (Aug 2017): the Cook Islands parliament began hearing submissions on the Crimes Bill replacing the 1969 Act; the Te Tiare Association (LGBTI community group) made a submission supporting decriminalisation.

records.name: Colombia
records.summary:
Colombia has one of Latin America's strongest legal frameworks — Constitutional Court legal gender recognition since 1993 (no surgery required, based on self-recognition), "trans" and "non-binary" ID markers (November 2025), a Comprehensive Trans Law being legislated (2025), marriage equality (2016), and a Constitutional Court ruling protecting a trans inmate from prison violence. President Petro's government is pro-LGBTIQ+.

But the law-versus-practice gap is extreme and violent. More than 40 trans women were killed in a single year, with armed groups running "social cleansing" campaigns (Caquetá) and posting kill-lists targeting specific LGBTQ individuals ("All will be military targets"). Sara Millerey, a trans woman, was tortured and murdered in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, with a viral video of the assault. The UN Independent Expert urged Colombia to "close the gap between laws and lived realities amid rising violence."

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, Bogotá's Chapinero district is a well-established LGBTQ+ area. The armed-group violence is concentrated in conflict regions and targets local communities, not tourists — but the organized targeting is a distinctive, severe concern.

sources.claim: El País (April 2025): the transphobic murder of Sara Millerey, 32, in Bello, Antioquia - thrown into a creek with fractured limbs and left to drown, filmed - shocked Colombia and terrified the trans community; her family demands justice.

CNN (Aug 2025): 'Sara Millerey's brutal murder shocked Colombia. The killings didn't stop there' — investigation into continued attacks and killings of trans women and LGBT people with little accountability.

The Guardian (July 2024): more than 40 trans women were killed in Colombia the previous year; armed groups in Caquetá are threatening a wave of 'social cleansing' - trans women report being killed 'for what we are' and repeatedly forced to flee.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): strong legal protections - 1999 Constitutional Court rulings restricting nonconsensual intersex surgeries; same-sex marriage since 2011 (refusals illegal since 2016); adoption since 2015; simplified legal gender recognition since 2015; third-gender classification for nonbinary people recognised March 2022; 2025 court order against a volleyball league regulator for discrimination.

JURIST (May 2025): UN Independent Expert Graeme Reid, concluding a fact-finding mission across Colombia, praised legal reforms but warned of a stark gap between institutional progress and lived reality - discrimination and violence persist, particularly against trans women and those facing intersecting marginalisation (migrants, Indigenous people, youth, persons with disabilities).
Ambito Jurídico (in Spanish): Colombian court protected the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty - ruling on treatment of trans detainees.

International Business Times (June 2015): Colombia allowed trans people to change name and sex on ID cards without physical or psychiatric examinations - a notarised declaration replaces the previous 'cumbersome' process that involved judges ordering bodily inspections; Justice Minister Yesid Reyes approved the decree.

freshness.fact: Rights regime remains progressive (marriage since 2016, adoption since 2015); Constitutional Court protections for trans people detained/accused, as in the cited ruling, still stand.

records.name: Comoros
records.summary: Comoros is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code criminalises acts “contrary to morality or against nature” (2 years), enforced: two women were detained in June 2024 after asking an Islamic preacher to marry them, convicted in December 2024 (released for time served). No LGR; small conservative archipelago.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents that Comoros criminalises same-sex sexual activity (up to 3 years' imprisonment under the penal code).
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Dec 2024) covers a couple in Comoros released after a same-sex sentencing verdict.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Comoros: official assessment including the SOGI section - same-sex conduct criminalised (Article 300), societal discrimination, and the December 2024 conviction of a lesbian couple.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Comoros: general human-rights baseline (poor prisons, restrictions on movement/press/religion, discrimination against women) with limited LGBT-specific content.

Outright International country overview (March 2026): Article 300 of the 2020 penal code punishes 'any act of a sexual nature that is contrary to public decency or against nature' with 6 months to 2 years and fines; no SOGISC protections, no legal gender recognition, no intersex protections; in 2022 a leaked video allegedly led to the first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy; in June 2024 two women were arrested after asking an Islamic preacher to marry them (convicted December 2024, sentenced to time served); the government repeatedly refuses UN decriminalisation recommendations.
Washington Blade (Dec 2024): 'Comoros court convicts lesbian couple, sentences them to months in jail' — a court upholds convictions of two women for same-sex relations despite an earlier acquittal.

freshness.fact: LGBTQ persons are still regularly prosecuted under the penal code alongside broad stigmatisation — 2023 State Dept/HDT profiles remain consistent.

records.name: Cabo Verde
records.summary: Cabo Verde is workable — Africa's most tolerant jurisdiction alongside South Africa's legal tier. Same-sex relations are legal; employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited; Praia and Mindelo host visible Pride events; the culture is notably relaxed by regional standards. No explicit GI protections and no LGR statute (administrative practice unclear), but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations not criminalised in Cabo Verde; employment protections based on sexual orientation (though gender identity/expression/sex characteristics not explicitly referenced); first Pride in 2013 (second African country to host one); 82% public acceptance of a 'homosexual' neighbour (2019-2021 polls); LGBTIQ organisations can register; no same-sex union recognition; committed at its 2024 UPR to improve protections; only African UN LGBTI Core Group member besides South Africa.

Equal Eyes (July 2018): Cape Verde's LGBTI Pride week in Praia - supported by the government's Institute for Gender Equality (ICIEG), Spanish Cooperation and City Hall; Pride began in Mindelo in 2013; activists campaign for same-sex marriage and an anti-LGBTIphobia non-discrimination law; slogan 'De boa com quem sou'.

Observador/Lusa (July 2017, in Portuguese): Cape Verde's PM said same-sex marriage is not on the government's political agenda, calling it 'opinion' - responding to LGBT community claims to union and marriage rights.

Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 (May 2020): 'All in this together' - Africans are tolerant on ethnic, religious and national differences but not sexual differences; Cabo Verde, Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe stand out as particularly tolerant countries; tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak even among younger respondents.

Rede Angola special (June 2016, in Portuguese): interview with Tchinda Andrade, the first person to come out publicly as trans in Cape Verde (1997, during Mindelo Carnival) - describes Cape Verde as 'a country with freedom relative to the LGBT mass', Mindelo as relaxed, though she experienced verbal violence and two physical attacks (possibly robbery-motivated).

records.name: Costa Rica
records.summary:
Costa Rica is workable for trans visitors — Central America's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber (Sala IV) with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. San José has a visible scene.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations legal since 1971; first Central American country with marriage equality (2020); since 2018 trans people can change legal gender without surgery or judicial intervention (Executive Decree N° 41173-MP instructs public institutions to update records per self-perceived gender identity); the state health system funds gender-affirming care; the progressive agenda faces increasing conservative resistance and paralysis.
ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Costa Rica: documents LGBTI-related legal frameworks — status of same-sex conduct, gender recognition and protections.

UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, report on her July 2023 visit to Costa Rica (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024): praised near-universal health coverage and good practices including specific legislation; concerned about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups; recommends intersectional data collection and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

GayLawNet Costa Rica laws page: age of consent 18 for same-sex couples (2008); survivor's pensions extended to same-sex couples (2016-2018, Ministry of Labor and Social Security); documents the incremental legal recognition timeline.

PinkNews (May 2008): Costa Rica officially recognised IDAHO Day (International Day Against Homophobia) - President Óscar Arias and the Health Minister directed public institutions to support anti-homophobia activities; credited to LGBT organisation CIPAC's advocacy.

The Tico Times (May 2014): social-conservative lawmakers were incensed when President Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial for IDAHOT - calling it a 'provocation' while a civil-unions bill was pending; documents the conservative resistance within Costa Rican politics.
